rv.q: When focused on the crux of the matter – to whom does art belong? – it's at its most compelling.

With the exception of Shostakovich’s later debates with the imagined character Katya, the play can feel surprisingly underpowered, though it will prompt many of us to dig out his music and read up on his difficult artistic life in the repressive Stalinist regime.
It is a competent biography of a complex and interesting character, but it lacks a bit of zest and never quite hits the right note.
In the effort to encapsulate so much of the tumultuous political and social context, what is ironically lost in this formal, traditional narrative is the central figure.
Other than this, the evening is neither offensive nor intriguing, but largely forgettable, a shame given what it might have been.

Unfortunately, the writers have simply pieced together a hotch-potch jigsaw of Shostakovich’s key life moments and then created a chatty script in the hopes it will serve to bring the great man’s travails to life for a presumably under-informed audience.
The reality of Holy Fool is that this is a boring play, both dramatically and conceptually.
Holy Fool is poignant, intelligent and unexpectedly funny.
Holy Fool is an immensely enjoyable and enlightening production, aided by the relief we bear a mere fraction of the pressure that Mitya would have been under all those years ago.
The theme of the play is as relevant today as it was in Shostakovich’s time.
This is the lightly fictionalised story of the agonies faced by the composer Dimitri Shostakovich as he struggled to retain artistic freedom in Stalin’s Soviet Union.
I congratulate the Park and director Kate Fahy for this informative production and would welcome seeing it again.
Under Kate Fahy's direction this horror is brilliantly staged – a single, harsh spotlight and off-stage whispers laden with threat.
For any history buffs and fans of classical music, this is the show for you.
There is much to admire here: a strong ensemble and a story that places artistic freedom, morality and survival under uncomfortable scrutiny.
For a story about one of the twentieth century's greatest composers, this feels like a missed opportunity.
Still, the performances are beautifully judged, Kate Fahy's direction is clear, and the lighting and projections are used effectively.
But the overall effect of the production is rather incoherent and incomplete.
I feel there is real potential here, but it is disappointing that it left so little of a mark on me.

Holy Fool is not without its high notes, and there is some genuine potential shining through, however in its current form remains largely forgettable, a shame given what the bones of a much stronger final product might have been.
Bending from a political thriller into a last-minute story of friendship, and not quite going into enough detail to be passable as a biographical piece, Holy Fool lacks a clear structure or climax.

Underground resistance and the human spirit is the story told here in an extremely well created and performed piece of work, with strong character acting and wry, comic moments to leaven the harsh story.
It is a well-researched and finely crafted script, penned by Rosalind Adler and Lea Sellers, which never feels too bloated despite the almost forty-year span of the piece.
For me, Holy Fool is at its strongest in the first act, where tension builds steadily due to the fear of living under an unpredictable regime.
For a play about one of the 20th century’s most significant composers, that feels like a considerable omission.
Although fused with witty lines and passionate performances, this is still too thin a story for its two-hour-and-30-minute running time.
Eventually, Holy Fool is nothing but a superficial, unenticing, and painfully boring piece, whose only appeal is the name it intends to honour — and fails to do so miserably.

cn.t: Critics find Holy Fool's exploration of Shostakovich under Stalin dramatically unfocused and overlong, though some praise its timely examination of art versus tyranny and strong performances that bring moments of compelling tension to the composer's perilous story.
